assert

uh-SURT — rhymes with 'dessert'; someone who asserts serves up their opinion with confidence. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To assert is to state a fact forcefully and with confidence.

The scientist continued to assert that the results were accurate, even as critics raised objections.

Example

A new employee is blamed for a mistake she didn't make. Instead of staying quiet, she calmly but firmly asserts the truth in front of the whole team — exactly what really happened and why she isn't at fault.

She speaks up firmly and confidently rather than letting the blame stand. Unlike 'mention,' which is casual, to assert means to state a claim with real conviction.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

declare: To declare is to state something openly and formally, making it public and definite: officials declare a winner, a country declares a holiday. To assert is to state a fact forcefully because you stand behind it, especially when someone doubts or challenges you.

insist: To insist is to keep stating or demanding something firmly, refusing to back down when others push against you. To assert is to put a claim forward forcefully in the first place; insisting is what asserting becomes once resistance appears and you hold your ground.

affirm: To affirm is to state that something is true, often calmly confirming what was already said or believed. To assert is more forceful: you push a claim forward with confidence and stand behind it even when others question it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deny: to state that something is not true

doubt: to feel uncertain about the truth of something

Where it sits · how forcefully it is said

mention → assert → demand

mention vs. assert: Mention is weaker than assert — mentioning something is casual, while asserting means stating it forcefully and standing behind it.

demand vs. assert: Demand is stronger than assert: asserting is stating something with confidence, but demanding requires an immediate response or action from someone else.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — as- (ad-): to (Latin)

root — -sert-: to join, to put in order (Latin)

Put it together: Latin asserere combined ad- (to) with serere (to join, to arrange in a row). To assert something is to firmly put a claim forward, joining your words to a stated position.

Use the root in a new word: insert: She decided to insert one more sentence into her essay before submitting it.
